nameStory: The 'dwarf' in dwarf morning-glory refers to its compact, low-growing habit compared to the tall, climbing vines we usually associate with morning-glories. The 'tricolor' part of its scientific name hints at its most stunning feature – flowers that display three distinct colors in beautiful concentric rings, creating a bull's-eye pattern that's impossible to miss.
description: Dwarf morning-glory is a small, spreading annual plant that stays close to the ground rather than climbing like its famous cousins. This Mediterranean native produces eye-catching funnel-shaped flowers with distinctive three-color patterns – typically blue petals with white centers and yellow throats. The plant forms low mats or mounds, rarely growing taller than 12 inches, making it look more like a colorful ground cover than a typical morning-glory vine.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Stunning funnel-shaped blooms about 1-2 inches across with three distinct color zones – usually deep blue or purple petals, a bright white ring in the middle, and a sunny yellow center that feels slightly fuzzy to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing, bushy plant that spreads outward rather than climbing, forming dense mats that stay under a foot tall with stems that feel slightly sticky when handled

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval to lance-shaped leaves arranged alternately along the stems, with a soft, slightly fuzzy texture and no teeth along the edges

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round seed capsules that split open when ripe to reveal dark brown or black seeds about the size of peppercorns

habitat: In New England, dwarf morning-glory is primarily found in cultivated gardens, especially rock gardens and sunny borders where it's grown as an ornamental annual. Occasionally it may escape cultivation and appear in disturbed soils, sunny waste areas, or along roadsides, particularly in warmer, well-drained spots.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms up, producing small seedlings with their first oval leaves appearing in May.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time from June through August, when the spectacular tricolor flowers open in the morning and close by afternoon on hot days.
seasonality.fall: Flowering continues into early fall until first frost kills the plants. Seed capsules ripen and split open, releasing next year's seeds.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely with frost, leaving only seeds in the soil to germinate the following spring.

funFact: Unlike most morning-glories that open at dawn and close by noon, dwarf morning-glory flowers stay open longer on cloudy days – they're actually responding to light intensity rather than just time of day, making them nature's own solar-powered timekeepers!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small garden flowers, but the distinctive three-color bull's-eye pattern is unique among New England plants. Remember: if it looks like a tiny morning-glory with perfect color rings and doesn't climb, you've found dwarf morning-glory.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a morning-glory, dwarf morning-glory belongs to the bindweed genus (Convolvulus) rather than the true morning-glory genus (Ipomoea). This naming confusion exists because both groups are closely related members of the bindweed family and share similar trumpet-shaped flowers.
compareHints: Dwarf morning-glory differs dramatically from its only New England relative, field bindweed, by staying low and bushy rather than climbing, and by having much showier tricolored flowers instead of field bindweed's plain white or pale pink blooms. Field bindweed is also a persistent perennial weed, while dwarf morning-glory is an annual that's much easier to control.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Field bindweed is the most common Convolvulus species in New England, while its relative dwarf morning-glory (Convolvulus tricolor) is mainly found in gardens as an ornamental with distinctive blue, white, and yellow flowers.
